title: Skincare routine basics (and Korean multi-step routines)
question_forms: What skincare routine is right for Black skin?
What skincare routine should Black men follow?
Does Korean skincare work for Black skin?
How do I get glowing, clear skin on dark skin?
How do I repair my skin barrier and stop over-exfoliating?
tradition_says: A long routine of steps, serums and exfoliants is sold as the way to clear, glowing skin, and scrubbing is often treated as what dark skin needs.

layer1.plain_answer: A short routine is what dermatologist guidance recommends: gentle cleanser, moisturiser and sunscreen. Scrubbing irritates and over-exfoliating is a common reason people see a dermatologist. I found no human study showing a long multi-step routine, Korean or otherwise, improves dark skin. Stop any product that burns or stings.

do.text: Cleanse gently with warm water and your fingertips, not tools.

source.name: American Academy of Dermatology, "Skin care tips dermatologists use"

do.text: Use a fragrance-free moisturiser, with ceramides if your skin looks ashy.

source.name: American Academy of Dermatology, "Dry skin remedies for darker skin tones"

do.text: Apply sunscreen daily: SPF 30 or higher, broad-spectrum, water-resistant.

source.name: American Academy of Dermatology, "Skin care tips dermatologists use"

do.text: Choose products for your skin type: oily, dry, normal, combination or sensitive.

source.name: American Academy of Dermatology, "Skin care tips dermatologists use"

do.text: If a product irritates your skin, stop using it right away.

source.name: American Academy of Dermatology, "Dermatologist-recommended skin care for your 20s"

avoid.text: Scrubbing: it irritates and can worsen any skin condition, including acne.

source.name: American Academy of Dermatology, "Skin care tips dermatologists use"

avoid.text: Overusing exfoliating products you see on social media: dermatologists frequently treat the damage.

source.name: American Academy of Dermatology, "Dermatologist-recommended skin care for your 20s"

avoid.text: Hot water and long baths on dry skin.

source.name: American Academy of Dermatology, "Dry skin remedies for darker skin tones"

avoid.text: Smoking: the AAD's skin-care tips say don't smoke.

source.name: American Academy of Dermatology, "Skin care tips dermatologists use"

see_someone_when: Skin is burning, stinging, peeling or breaking out after a product (stop it; pharmacist or doctor if it does not settle).
Dark patches, spots or irritation that a basic routine does not fix (doctor or dermatologist).
A skin change you are unsure about (doctor).

tier_driver: The claim people make is that a multi-step (for example Korean) routine, or any exfoliating routine, gives clearer or glowing dark skin: my search found nothing in humans. The basic-routine advice is guidance, not trial evidence.
tier_note: D because the headline claim people come with (the multi-step routine works for dark skin) has no human study in my search ("Korean skincare ten step routine evidence" returned nothing on PubMed; control: other PubMed searches in this session returned records). Would move with a trial of a routine against a simple one, reported by skin type. The moisturising trial is in the moisturising entry.
harm_note: The harm in this entry is irritation from over-exfoliating and too many actives (AAD guidance); not tested.
evidence_summary: AAD guidance for everyone: cleanse gently, moisturise, use sunscreen of SPF 30 or higher daily, match products to skin type, do not scrub, stop products that irritate. The AAD dry-skin page for darker skin tones adds ceramide moisturisers to reduce the whitish look of dry skin. I found no trial of a Korean-style multi-step routine and none comparing routines by skin colour; my one PubMed search on it returned nothing.
measured_variables: Skin type (oily, dry, normal, combination, sensitive)
gaps: Fact-check 12 Nov: all three AAD pages behind the do and avoid lines re-opened and each line found on them (the dry-skin page describes a whitish or greyish look on melanin-rich skin, not the word ashy). Untested: the long routine against the short routine; which actives (niacinamide, vitamin C, azelaic acid, retinoids) work on dark skin beyond the dark marks entry; men-specific skincare (no source found, so guidance is general). Barrier repair: the AAD advice to stop irritants and moisturise is guidance, with no trial opened. Founder: none.
